content: When individuals with both HIV and tuberculosis (TB) are treated with a boosted protease inhibitor, rifampicin may need to be substituted with rifabutin at a daily dose of 150 mg. If rifabutin is unavailable, lopinavir/ritonavir can be used during TB treatment by either doubling the standard dose or increasing the boosting dose of ritonavir. When rifampicin is co-administered with dolutegravir, the dolutegravir dose should be increased to 50 mg twice daily, provided there is no resistance to integrase strand transfer inhibitors. If resistance is present, this combination should be avoided. In pediatric patients, dolutegravir or raltegravir should be dosed twice daily for an additional two weeks after rifampicin use has ended. If raltegravir is considered (only in specific circumstances), the dose should be doubled to 800 mg twice daily, as standard doses of raltegravir with rifampicin have been shown to be suboptimal. Rifampicin reduces exposure to tenofovir alafenamide and tenofovir, but recent data indicate that intracellular levels of tenofovir diphosphate (the active form) remain four times higher than those achieved with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, even without rifampicin. This suggests that tenofovir alafenamide at 25 mg once daily with rifampicin may be acceptable under special circumstances when used in first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART). However, there is currently no data on virological outcomes with tenofovir alafenamide at 25 mg once or twice daily with rifampicin. In individuals with HIV and extensively drug-resistant or multidrug-resistant TB who are receiving drugs like bedaquiline and delamanid, caution is advised when co-administering protease inhibitors due to the risk of QT-interval prolongation. Additionally, as bedaquiline is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4, its concurrent use with efavirenz may reduce bedaquiline concentrations, potentially leading to loss of efficacy; therefore, this combination should be avoided. Treatment of latent TB infection with isoniazid (300 mg) and rifapentine (600 mg) daily for four weeks or once weekly for three months is not recommended for individuals receiving protease inhibitors or nevirapine due to the risk of HIV virological failure. There is no evidence to suggest that dosage adjustments for rifapentine, dolutegravir, or raltegravir are necessary for patients on these regimens. However, when rifampicin is used, the doses of dolutegravir, raltegravir, and tenofovir alafenamide should be doubled when combined with isoniazid and rifapentine daily for four weeks, whereas standard doses can be used with isoniazid and rifapentine once weekly for three months. Pharmacovigilance systems, which are typically designed to monitor side effects, adverse reactions, and drug interactions, should be expanded to address the growing issue of substandard and counterfeit medicines and to monitor the development of drug resistance. Substandard medicines have caused preventable deaths and iatrogenic side effects. Routine monitoring of resistance should be incorporated into the early stages of research and development. A clear distinction must be made between adverse events and adverse drug reactions when assessing their severity and relationship to a product. Once an adverse event is detected, its maximum severity should be graded according to international standards, and its causality should be determined. Serious adverse events should be investigated and reported promptly. Quality assurance and regulatory mechanisms are critically important, and pharmacovigilance systems in visceral leishmaniasis (VL)-endemic countries require improvement, with a multi-disease approach integrated into their design. Issues such as toxicity, adherence, treatment response, and resistance have impacted treatment programs, and reporting systems for these events should be strengthened. Multidisciplinary national pharmacovigilance centers should be established and their capacity enhanced to regularly analyze safety data, identify and review signals, generate hypotheses, and ensure consistent reporting and feedback. Post-licensing clinical trials, case-control studies, and active population-based evaluations of marketed products should be included in pharmacovigilance methods. The WHO Drug Monitoring System, which includes 170 member countries, provides a global network for pharmacovigilance. All countries should establish national pharmacovigilance centers to record adverse drug reactions and contribute to the WHO global database, VigiBase, which has been used to monitor adverse reactions to antileishmanial medicines, including those with serious outcomes. Monitoring and evaluation of leishmaniasis control programs aim to collect, process, analyze, and disseminate relevant information, verify that activities are implemented as planned, provide feedback to improve future planning, and document whether strategies achieve expected outcomes. Monitoring involves routine tracking of program performance through record-keeping, reporting, surveillance, and periodic surveys. Indicators include input, process, output, and outcome measures. Evaluation assesses the impact and effectiveness of interventions over time. A monitoring and evaluation framework can provide reliable information at local, national, or international levels. HIV data should be integrated into VL program data management systems and vice versa. The WHO Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTD) roadmap for 2021–2030 has set a target for global elimination of VL as a public health problem (defined as a case fatality rate of less than 1% due to primary VL) by 2030. This target should encourage national programs to strengthen leishmaniasis surveillance and include HIV-VL variables and indicators. Factors contributing to antimicrobial resistance include suboptimal treatment regimens, inadequate dosing or duration, irregular treatment, use of substandard medicines, poor surveillance of treatment outcomes, lack of biomarkers for parasite resistance, and absence of national plans for drug resistance surveillance. A study in South Asia found that low treatment efficacy of antimonials for VL in HIV-negative patients was associated with irregular treatment and incomplete dosing, which likely contributed to the development of resistance. Although multidrug therapy can reduce the likelihood of selecting drug-resistant parasites, decreased cure rates may signal emerging resistance. WHO recommends counseling and follow-up for all VL cases and routine monitoring of cure rates. Treatment efficacy and clinical outcomes will be regularly evaluated to monitor potential drug resistance. Laboratory surveillance for drug resistance should be integrated into national antimicrobial resistance plans. Monitoring access to leishmanial medicines should be strengthened, including pricing, registration, drug policies, and quality assurance. National leishmaniasis control programs should adopt recommendations on VL in relevant policies and guidelines. Stakeholder consultations, including affected patients and communities, can improve uptake and dissemination of guidelines. Measures should be taken to expand access to treatment and services for VL patients, including timely treatment of VL episodes, management of opportunistic infections, nutritional support, access to ART, and follow-up. Secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities should be equipped with diagnostics, essential medicines, and adequate human resources to manage such patients. HIV-VL management requires a comprehensive, multi-pronged approach with coordinated guidelines for VL and HIV programs. Globally, nearly one-third of VL patients are unaware of their HIV status. In highly VL-endemic states like Bihar and Jharkhand in India, over 90% of VL patients detected in 2020 knew their HIV status. Training for healthcare professionals, community health workers, and at-risk populations on VL-HIV co-infection should be customized and widely implemented. Coordination between programs for HIV, TB, leishmaniasis, and vector-borne disease control is essential in areas where these conditions overlap. Efficient links and integrated program management should be established to control both conditions effectively. Optimal management of VL-HIV co-infection aims to cure VL and achieve undetectable viral loads through early ART initiation. Late diagnosis of leishmaniasis in people living with HIV is challenging, and awareness of this co-infection must be increased among healthcare professionals. Operational research should focus on developing screening strategies in high HIV-VL prevalence areas and integrating relevant components of VL and HIV programs. Improved diagnostic tests, biomarkers, and criteria for cure are urgently needed. Long-term follow-up of treated patients will help understand the development of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL). The role of TB as a co-morbid condition in VL-HIV patients should be further studied, as it significantly impacts outcomes. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in VL-HIV co-infection requires detailed prospective studies to characterize its clinical features and incidence. Enhanced understanding of the epidemiology and progression of VL in HIV patients, along with improved biomarkers, will be critical for effective management.
